title: Joint, marginal, conditional & Bayes
blurb: Sum rule, product rule, independence, Bayes theorem

hook.title: The smoke alarm that cries wolf
hook.text: Your house has a smoke alarm that is **90% accurate**: it rings in 90% of real fires. But it also rings 8% of the time when you merely burn toast. Fires are rare (2% of days). The alarm rings. *How worried should you be?* Most people say “90%”. The truth is far lower, because you must combine what the alarm says (the **likelihood**) with what you believed before it rang (the **prior**).
hook.recall: Remember the smoke alarm: a ringing alarm doesn't replace your prior, it updates it. Posterior ∝ likelihood × prior, normalised by the evidence.

explore.intro: Start on the joint table, then open the Bayes tab.
tasks: Joint tab: click a weather row. Which rule turns the joint table into $p(x\mid y)$? Make the table independent (every $p(x,y)=p(x)p(y)$) using the +/− buttons.
Bayes tab: set the prior to 0.02, sensitivity 0.9, false-positive rate 0.08. Then lower the prior to 0.01. What happens to the posterior?
explore.takeaway: Sum rule → marginal. Product rule → $p(x,y)=p(y|x)p(x)$. Bayes' theorem rearranges it: $p(x|y)=p(y|x)p(x)/p(y)$. The evidence $p(y)$ is a sum over all the ways to get the observation.

build.explanation: $p(x|y)=\dfrac{p(y|x)p(x)}{p(y)}$: posterior, likelihood, prior and evidence, exactly the naming on the slide.

questions.prompt: Smoke-alarm numbers: prior $p(\text{fire})=0.02$, $p(\text{ring}\mid\text{fire})=0.9$, $p(\text{ring}\mid\text{no fire})=0.08$. Compute $p(\text{fire}\mid\text{ring})$ (3 decimals).
questions.explanation: Evidence: $p(\text{ring})=0.9(0.02)+0.08(0.98)=0.0964$. Posterior $=0.018/0.0964\approx0.187$. Under 19%, not 90%, because false alarms from the many non-fire days dominate.

questions.prompt: In $p(x|y)=\dfrac{p(y|x)\,p(x)}{p(y)}$, the term $p(y|x)$ is called the:
questions.explanation: $p(y|x)$ is how likely the observation $y$ is under hypothesis $x$: the alarm's 90% accuracy, in the smoke-alarm story.

questions.prompt: Suppose $x$ and $y$ are independent. Which statement is FALSE?
questions.explanation: Independence means that learning $x$ tells you nothing about $y$: $p(y|x)=p(y)$, not $p(x)$. In the alarm story, independence would mean ringing tells you nothing about fire.

questions.prompt: Sum rule: $p(x=a,y=1)=0.12$, $p(x=a,y=2)=0.18$, $p(x=a,y=3)=0.10$ (these are all the values of $y$). What is the marginal $p(x=a)$?
questions.explanation: $p(x)=\sum_y p(x,y)=0.12+0.18+0.10=0.40$. Marginalising adds up every way to see $x=a$, like counting every kind of toast-or-fire that could ring the alarm.

questions.prompt: $x$ = image pixels, $y$ = weather. A student says: *“$p(x|y)$ and $p(y|x)$ are the same thing, they’re both just x and y together.”* What’s wrong?
options: $p(x|y)$ is the probability of pixels given the weather; $p(y|x)$ is the probability of weather given the image. They are different distributions, linked by Bayes
They differ only when $x$ and $y$ are independent
questions.explanation: Order matters: $P(\text{ring}\mid\text{fire})=0.9$ but $P(\text{fire}\mid\text{ring})\approx0.19$, the whole point of the smoke-alarm story. Bayes' theorem converts one into the other.
